thread.title: Is There A Legitimate Rationale For Berkshire Buybacks? Yes, And They Come With A Treasure Trove Of Buffett Thinking - Berkshire Hathaway A (NYSE:BRK.A)

author: Jim Sloan
title: Is There A Legitimate Rationale For Berkshire Buybacks? Yes, And They Come With A Treasure Trove Of Buffett Thinking - Berkshire Hathaway A (NYSE:BRK.A)
text:
Matt Levine doesn't like Buffett's Berkshire (NYSE: BRK.B ) buybacks.
Don't get me wrong. I like Matt Levine's Money Stuff blog. Something got me to sign on a few months ago, and I think most of his pieces are terrific. His specialty is thought pieces about companies and executives who do absurd things (think Elon Musk). Levine is a gadfly. He calls out both scandalous corporate behavior and the numbskull acceptance of it. His writing combines irreverence and sharp insight into corporate shenanigans, and a devastating analysis of "Netflix Theory" is contained in the same piece which prompted this article.
With that as a disclaimer, I have to say that he made a surpassingly silly case against Buffett's Berkshire buybacks. His argument struck me as (1) asking a potentially interesting question but (2) missing some major factors to be considered. His major argument attacks a straw man - "Buffett the market timer." In the process, he missed the chance to discover some very interesting insights into Buffett's thought process which contains some actionable elements.
Here's Levine's Argument Against The Buybacks
When a company has more cash than it can put into valuable projects, it is too big, and should shrink by giving some money back to shareholders so they can put it into valuable projects; or When a company's stock is an attractive investment, it should buy some of that stock.
Model 1 is fairly conventional corporate finance. A company raises money from investors to do a thing, it does the thing, the thing generates money, it uses the money to reinvest in doing the thing. If the thing works well it will generate more money than the company needs to reinvest in doing it, and the company should give the money back to its investors, both because they may have better ideas for what to do with the money than the company does (since the company really specializes in doing the one thing) and because after all they invested in the company in the expectation of getting their money back with a profit...Model 2, on the other hand, is a bit silly. It is hard for anyone to time the market. It is particularly hard for corporate executives to time the market in their own stocks, because corporate executives tend to be selected in part for their enthusiasm about their companies. Also companies tend to want to buy back stock when they have a lot of cash, which tends to be when things are going well, which in cyclical businesses means that they tend to buy high and sell low. Plus if companies are good at timing buybacks of their own stock, that's kind of a mixed bag; it suggests that they're using their privileged view of inside information to trade against their shareholders. On the other hand there's Berkshire Hathaway Inc. It is hard to argue for Model 1 there: Berkshire doesn't specialize in building one particular type of widget; it's more or less an investment firm. It is run by Warren Buffett and his handpicked lieutenants, and there is good reason to think that they are better at investing than you are. If they happen to have "struggled to find ways to invest a swelling cash pile that has surpassed $100 billion each of the past five quarters," well, so would you have. "Berkshire is too big and so should return money to shareholders so they can find good investment ideas because Warren Buffett can't" just feels kind of wrong. It might be right! ("Even he can't keep up with all the cash Berkshire generates," writes my Bloomberg Opinion colleague Tara Lachapelle, who has some ideas about what he should do with it.) But it feels presumptuous to think that Berkshire's shareholders would be better stewards of their cash than Buffett is. So that leaves market timing as an explanation. Berkshire bought back $928 million of stock in August, with a new policy that allows for more flexibility in market timing: The firm's old policy limited repurchases to when the shares traded at less than a 20 percent premium to book value. Now, Buffett and Vice Chairman Charlie Munger can decide when the stock is trading at less than what they believe is the intrinsic value. "The shares have traded below his average purchase price for much of the past two weeks," though, so even Buffett's market timing isn't perfect.
Model 1: Muddled Writing Equals Muddled Thinking The funny thing is that when I read Levine's discussion of Model 1, I can't tell whether he is making the positive case or the negative case. The latter, I guess. The only moment when I have a clear sense of the side Levine comes down on is the line that it is "hard to argue for Model 1." His major problem with the buybacks seems to be that Berkshire is not a company which specializes in producing a particular type of widget.
Well, duh. But this is also true of almost all large companies. It makes no sense as an argument unless you want to try to argue that Procter & Gamble ( PG ), just to serve as an example, makes a single product. I guess they do if soap and toothpaste are essentially the same thing. Gosh, maybe they sort of are. I guess the legitimacy of buybacks at Procter & Gamble hinges on whether I am willing to brush my teeth with Tide and wash my laundry with Crest.
As for Levine's argument that Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK.A )( BRK.B ) is "more or less an investment firm," you might have said that 20 years ago if willing to ignore the insurance businesses. Berkshire is now a conglomerate, sometimes characterized as a financial and sometimes as an industrial, made up of more than 80 operating entities with decentralized operational control but centralized capital allocation. It also happens to have a large stock portfolio.
As a whole, the many separate entities of Berkshire throw off more cash than they can productively reinvest - something north of two billion a month and rising. Yes, Berkshire doesn't specialize in building one particular type of widget. You can certainly argue that one wouldn't eat a locomotive or make electricity with Dairy Queen sundaes. Yet the differences of the various widgets produced by all large companies are merely a matter of degree. Capital allocation presents a universal problem whether you are a giant conglomerate like Berkshire or the latest one-idea startup. All companies must decide how to make rational use of capital.
To argue that Berkshire differs from any other company which takes money from investors to do a thing, does the thing, which then does well and generates more cash than needed for reinvestment, is to make a distinction without a difference. Like every other business Berkshire at the top level is in the business of capital allocation. It just does it better than almost anyone else and draws from a wider range of options.
For a moment, I thought Levine was about to argue that dividends in general were a more legitimate form of cash return than buybacks, but he doesn't quite make that argument. If he had done so, I would have referred to Buffett's clear and elegant counterargument presented in his famous 1977 Fortune article which I cited and linked in this article on the subject. From every standpoint, including taxes and fairness to continuing shareholders, the option to realize cash by selling shares has a more efficient and fairer outcome than cash dividends. Buybacks are merely an extension of this argument, with remaining holders again benefiting by owning a larger share of the company.
Model 2: Still Muddled And Misinformed Model 2 makes as little sense as Model 1. Buffett is a value investor. Or you might call him a GARP investor - growth at a reasonable price. There is nothing about Berkshire's buyback policy that has anything whatever to do with "timing the market." Buffett has never been a "market timer," although from time to time he has taken action and written about his view of market valuations at or close to turning points. If buying things when they are cheap or holding cash when they are dear is "market timing," Buffett would have to plead guilty. Otherwise, Buffett's timing is purely coincidental.
I think there's a more encompassing way of thinking about the Buffett buybacks. Buffett has a clear hierarchy for actions with spare cash - internal reinvestment being first and accretive acquisitions second. Buying publicly traded stocks comes third, and buying back shares of Berkshire itself comes last. In spite of this, buying back Berkshire shares amounts to a composite of the other three uses of free cash:
Effectively putting money back into his own business by spreading its cash flow over fewer shares. Enjoying the major benefits from buying whole companies, namely complete control over cash flows plus avoidance of any tax consequences either to Berkshire itself or to continuing holders. Simply buying an attractive stock traded on the public market, but which happens to be the one company he knows best. That's the rationale for the legitimacy of Berkshire buybacks. Matt Levine, I suspect, thinks more like a writer and critic and less like an investor. Where the stock trades a month after the buybacks would matter only if you were a trader hoping to sell for a quick profit. Buffett's buybacks are a capital allocation decision, not a trading decision. The market price matters only as a measure of the business value of the stock bought.
Expanding Buffett's View Of Buybacks Buying back your own stock is just like buying any stock. There is no doubt that buybacks by many companies are done at bad prices and for bad reasons. The worst are done by companies which compensate high level employees with stock options and then buy back shares to offset the options, in the process diluting their shareholders. Berkshire Hathaway does not employ stock options as compensation.
It is also true that many corporations buy back shares at high prices mainly to inflate earnings per share. Buffett is well aware of this problem. For years, he set low multiples of book value as the hurdle for buying back shares. In the last few years, he acknowledged that a true estimate of the value of Berkshire was beginning to pull away from book value. This happened because an increasing part of Berkshire earnings came from the cash flows of whole companies Berkshire had acquired. These companies continued in perpetuity to be carried on the books at their purchase price - an accounting convention. Meanwhile, their cash flows have grown enormously. Buffett was simply correcting a buyback hurdle that was irrationally low.
Buffett always looks at both risks and probable returns. For a number of reasons, his preference is to buy whole businesses over which he has full control and full access to the cash flow. He also pays close attention to taxes. He appreciates the fact that internal cash flows are not taxed twice like dividends. Buying something on the market, as with his huge purchases of Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), comes with real but fairly small tax consequences on the dividend, but the tax consequences on capital gains are much greater than those for an individual investor. Wholly-owned businesses will never trade again, so the problem of capital gains taxes does not come up.
Buffett is pleased to redeploy cash flow internally to the advantage of whichever wholly owned businesses have the strongest probable rate of return on incremental capital. Buying back shares of Berkshire itself is a last resort, but it folds in many of the advantages of internal reinvestment. The difference is that it involves weighing his estimate of Berkshire's intrinsic value against any and all external opportunities. He has therefore been very conservative about Berkshire buybacks in the past. So, what has changed prompting the current modification of buyback rules and the recent purchases?
Buffett knows an enormous amount about Berkshire and its many businesses. He knows it as a business, and he understands the persistence of its rising cash flow as well as the right scale of risk band to put around his best estimate. In buying publicly traded shares or whole businesses, there's always something you don't know. It's like the little defects a house seller knows and the buyer doesn't. In buying back Berkshire shares, Buffett is simply buying shares of a business which is listed on the exchange, but which he knows as intimately as a house seller knows his house.
Deconstructing Buffett Thinking In Past Deals Buffett deals often convey a lot of collateral information. The predominant trend in his deals over the past two decades has involved buying industrial companies which could be expected to grow like the US economy but perhaps at a slightly greater rate - companies like Burlington Northern Santa Fe and Precision Castparts.
Both these deals were part of a tilt toward acquisitions which required major inputs of capital but with a relatively secure return - a huge departure from past acquisitions like Dairy Queen and public stock holdings like Coca-Cola ( KO ), which throw off a huge amount of cash with very little investment required. The more recent deals reflect a turn away from companies with high present ROIC but no place to reinvest with similar return. The point that is easy to miss is that buying a large industrial company serves to dilute the importance of subsidiaries like Dairy Queen or stock holdings like Coke.
There is always a structural message implicit in deals and large stock purchases. Apple probably reflects a re-balancing and updating of his holdings toward an area of branded technology that he feels he understands. Apple is an attempt to pull Berkshire into the contemporary economy via a consumer/tech company driven by a combination of brand power and technology. It gently shifts the structure of Berkshire.
Buffett's most interesting structural bet involved the 1998 purchase of General Re. It was not a secret that he believed the market of the dot.com era to be absurdly expensive. Let's give him credit for being right about that, although at the time he was seen as a washed-up old fogy. But what could he do about the valuation of the market? Stocks he owned like Coca-Cola had been carried along with the market to absurd heights, but to sell them meant surrendering over a third of his capital (capital gains within companies being taxed as ordinary income at the then rate of 35%). He also would have had to give up dividends which by then produced a high return on his original investment and which when held inside other companies are taxed very lightly.
General Re presented a solution. Gen Re was a reinsurance stalwart which set capital aside for future claims with a large bond portfolio - about $22 billion. Buying Gen Re shifted the bond/stock ratio within Berkshire toward bonds, which Buffett told attendees of that year's Sun Valley conference that he was "not unhappy with," adding "It did have the effect of a portfolio allocation change." That's Buffett's kind of second-level thinking and shows how carefully he considers the question of Berkshire's overall makeup.
Informed readers may be aware that while the Gen Re acquisition solved one problem, it created a few others. Gen Re came with derivative contracts which Buffett seems not to have examined closely, and which gave him years of headaches. It also suffered from some badly priced underwriting. That's the problem of the other fellow knowing his house in a way you can't. We investors are always the other fellow.
What eventually bothered Buffett more than these slip-ups was the fact that he paid for the purchase of Gen Re in Berkshire shares. While Gen Re righted the ship and did reasonably well in the long term, Berkshire Hathaway as a whole did far better. Ironically, buying Gen Re ended up diluting the growth of Berkshire's other businesses. Buffett didn't miss the implications of that.
The Gen Re experience drove home two things: (1) you can change the shape of your company with an acquisition, and (2) Berkshire shares are a precious currency and the value of their future prospects must be kept in mind. Both these insights have had an impact on Buffett's subsequent decisions, including, particularly, the present buybacks.
What Buffett Is Telling Us Now Seen in context of the trend in the last two decades of Buffett deals and also the lessons learned from specific deals both large and small, it's possible to tease out some current Buffett views of both Berkshire and the market. I'll present them in the form of a list.
Buffett is unable to find many things to buy in the present market. Reread the preceding sentence. It is not a market timing decision or a comment on the future of the economy. It means exactly what it says. Buffett just thinks the present market offers slim pickings for a value investor. Buffett is finding it even harder to find whole companies to buy. His criteria include being a good or great business at a reasonable price and being available for purchase with a single offer (no negotiation) and without the need for a hostile bid. One of the suggestions cited by Matt Levine's colleague Tara Lachapelle is Parker-Hannifin ( PH ), which might meet his first criterion. PH has outstanding management which has been fair and friendly to shareholders and has been prudent enough to minimize the impact of economic downturns. I own it in size in family accounts but would add strongly if another down leg of this correction made it 10-15% cheaper. From Buffett's perspective, the problem would be that PH has no major long term leader or owner with a large stake in the company - a person with whom he could discuss a deal. PH management is made up of engineers, not deal makers. Current management might reasonably argue that they are doing quite well as they are, thank you very much, and Buffett has always honored a gentlemanly no. Buffett has over $100 billion in cash earning the rate of short term T Bills, and he clearly feels pressure to do something better with it. At the same time, he doesn't wish to rush in and overpay, or undertake risks in a company about which he has imperfect information and understanding. The one company of which he has the best understanding of value and future prospects is the one he built himself. Buffett has no use whatever for bonds at the rates presently afforded. Period. For what it's worth, I am in total agreement. Buffett likes his own company. Knowing it from the inside out, he probably steps back a mile or two and says to himself, "Gee, out of all the things available on the exchange or in private hands, I don't see anything I really like better than my own company. Why not do the obvious thing? Why not employ capital so that I and other holders can own a little larger percentage of it?" Buffett also seems to like the overall makeup of the businesses within Berkshire. Berkshire has major holdings in insurance, energy (including utilities, power generation, and pipelines), industrials (including BNSF and Precision Castparts), housing and housing-related businesses, branded consumer businesses (including Apple), and financials. The above companies and industries are what he is buying when he buys back his own shares. They include a balanced portfolio of companies which are highly leveraged to the growth of the American economy and a few companies which are more stable. It is important news that he is happy with this mix of industries and demonstrates it by buying in stock which represents in aggregate cyclical growth companies. Investors and prospective investors in these industries should take note. In the past, he has taken actions which structurally serve to diversify away from his present businesses. He is not currently trying to diversify away from his present holdings. Buffett seems to have a long-term positive view of both housing-related companies and financials in general. He is certainly positioned to have a clear view into the workings of these businesses. What they share is being the cheapest areas of the current market. The fact that housing-related and financials are cheap may derive from the lingering bad feeling about their performance in the last great market crack-up. That's what happened with technology for more than a decade after the dot-com bubble and collapse. Buffett probably sees this as erroneous crowd behavior and feels that this concern is misplaced and presents an opportunity. He is well situated to know. (For what it's worth, I'm with him strongly on financials and a little less strongly on housing.) While I was working on this article, Berkshire's 13F was released and showed among other things a large purchase of JPMorgan ( JPM ), almost certainly a personal Buffett choice, as well as Travelers ( TRV ). Think about it. Berkshire is already chock full of banks and its core business is insurance. If Buffett is buying JPM and TRV, he must really love banks and casualty insurance businesses. He must think they are cheap, and he must have no fears about their future. He probably also loves the way each of them uses buybacks, especially Travelers, which has increased per share earnings and stock price at a high single digit rate for a decade without any top line growth. All the growth has come by reducing the share float with buybacks. What Buffett sees when he looks at this is underwriting discipline and shareholder friendliness. Conclusion What you do with the above projection of Buffett's thinking is up to each individual investor. It goes without saying that I think Buffett is still with it and better at making important decisions than ever. I'm less sure of his command in the area of technology, partly because I am unsure of my own opinions about the area.
I am strongly overweight by any standard in Berkshire B shares. I also have positions in every major bank except Citigroup ( C ) - no strong reason for its omission - and in both Travelers and Chubb ( CB ). I also own industrials such as United Technologies ( UTX ) and Parker-Hannifin. I bought them on the basis of my own analysis and judgment, being influenced by Buffett only at the level of fundamental principles. I dumped my home builders last February on a valuation basis and wrote about it on SA at the time.
My portfolio is a bit lopsided because made up of things about which I have knowledge and conviction and which were cheap when I bought them and remain cheap to fairly priced. It increases my confidence that Berkshire has a similar selection of wholly owned businesses and a somewhat lopsided portfolio not too different from mine. It reinforces my conviction further to see that Buffett is willing to buy more of it by buying back Berkshire shares.
Disclosure: I am/we are long BRK.B, CB, TRV. JPM, PH, UTX.
